summary: A humorous April 1st RFC that proposes a framework for detecting sarcasm in AI systems and guidelines for using sarcasm without offending. It is a joke, not a real specification.

plainLanguage.summary: A joke document about teaching computers to notice sarcasm, so you can tease them politely.

subtitle: A framework for detecting sarcasm in AI systems and using sarcasm respectfully.

tldr.problem: AI systems struggle to detect and interpret sarcasm, a form of language that relies heavily on context and tone, leading to misunderstandings.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9405 proposes the AI Sarcasm Detection Protocol (ASDP), which trains AI systems using labeled datasets of sarcastic and non-sarcastic language samples. The protocol uses natural language processing techniques such as machine learning and deep learning to extract linguistic patterns and contextual cues from text, then classifies the input as sarcastic or not sarcastic.
tldr.outcome: This April Fools' RFC provides a lighthearted technical approach to a real challenge in human-AI communication, with security considerations about adversarial attacks and privacy.

facts.label: Key techniques
facts.value: Support Vector Machines, Naive Bayes, Deep Learning

today: RFC 9405 is an Informational RFC published on April 1, 2023. It remains a humorous proposal exploring the challenge of sarcasm detection in AI, though it has not been standardized as a real protocol.

sections.title: The Sarcasm Challenge
sections.content: RFC 9405 is an April Fools' RFC that proposes a framework for detecting sarcasm in AI systems and guidelines for using sarcasm respectfully. The document notes that as AI becomes more integrated into daily life, effective communication with AI systems is important. However, sarcasm is difficult for AI to understand because it relies on context and tone to convey meaning opposite to the literal words. The RFC proposes training AI systems to recognize linguistic patterns and contextual cues that indicate sarcasm, improving their ability to understand human communication and avoiding misunderstandings.
sections.plainLanguage: Sarcasm is when you say the opposite of what you mean, often as a joke. Computers have a hard time understanding this. The RFC jokes that you can teach a computer to get the joke.

sections.title: The Sarcasm Detection Protocol
sections.content: The AI Sarcasm Detection Protocol (ASDP) consists of two main components: training data and a sarcasm detection algorithm. Training requires a diverse, labeled dataset of sarcastic and non-sarcastic language samples representative of the context in which the AI will operate. Labels can be binary (sarcasm or not) or graded (indicating degree of sarcasm). Popular machine learning techniques include Support Vector Machines, Naive Bayes, and Deep Learning models. The detection algorithm tokenizes input text, extracts features such as linguistic patterns (exaggeration, irony, understatement), contextual cues (quotation marks, emoticons), and sentiment analysis, then classifies the result.
sections.plainLanguage: To teach a computer about sarcasm, you collect many examples labeled as sarcastic or not, then use machine learning to find the patterns. The computer learns what linguistic and emotional clues mean someone is being sarcastic.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content: The RFC identifies three security concerns. Adversarial attacks can fool the algorithm by injecting non-sarcastic text with linguistic patterns common in sarcasm, causing false positives or negatives. Privacy risks arise if the training dataset contains sensitive or personal information. Malicious use could exploit sarcasm detection to manipulate or deceive individuals. To address these, the RFC recommends secure communication protocols such as TLS or HTTPS to protect requests and responses, and careful curation and protection of training datasets from unauthorized access. Interestingly, any vulnerabilities discovered can be logged using HTTP/2 or syslog, treating them as ordinary protocol traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Teaching a computer about sarcasm has risks: attackers could trick it, the training data might contain private information, and someone could use sarcasm detection to manipulate people. Use encrypted connections and keep the training data secret.
